newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Slow Telebras growth no problem - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Slow Telebras growth no problem - analysts.

text.p: Sluggish cellular and fixed line growth at Brazilian telecoms giant Telebras in 1997's first two months have not upset year-end forecasts for muscular growth in both areas, analysts said.

"I'm not worried," said Sergio Missima, a telecommunications sector analyst at local investment bank Banco Fator. Telebras last week released unaudited two-month results that showed a seven percent annualized growth in fixed lines and 26 percent hike in cellular subscribers in the January-February period.
Analysts told Reuters they are leaving unchanged their projections of 60-80 percent growth in cellular subscribers and a 12-18 percent rise in installed fixed lines this year at Telebras.

They said the relatively slow growth rate of new lines and subscribers in the two-month period was largely seasonal and surging growth was still foreseen, especially in cellular services, in the second half of 1997.
"I don't think we can annualize these (two-month) numbers," added Eduardo Munemori, an analyst at local investment bank Banco Pactual.
"We're going to have the start-up of a lot of cellular projects in the second half of the year," he said.

The federal Telebras system installed 78,000 lines in January and 74,000 lines in February, while its cellular network grew by 105,000 subscribers in the period. Installed fixed lines totalled 14.93 million and cellular subscribers reached 2.45 million by the end of 1996.

The slow rate of growth in the January-February period "is largely attributable to seasonality, with Telebras's first quarter growth rates historically being the most modest," U.S.-based Bear Stearns said in a report.

Analysts expect strong growth this year based on the large backlog of fixed-line contracts and a projected boom in the cellular services, as the company looks to compete for the first time against private cellular operators. Early in April, a privatization auction of Brazil's B Band cellular services drew bids from 15 consortia seeking to operate in nine of 10 service concession areas offered across Brazil.

Bear Stearns added that Telebras' two-month results also showed local traffic was flat and was likely to end 1997 that way, as a recent rate rebalancing raised "average local variable usage charges 57 percent as of May."
Telebras is slated to be broken up and sold off by the end of 1998, with long-distance unit Embratel and Sao Paulo area unit Telesp going to auction early next year.
